item.content:encoded:
jason (@jxnlco)

jason from the codex team here,
heres a draft on codex maxxing and the primatives i use on a daily basis

https://jxnl.github.io/blog/writing/2026/05/10/codex-maxxing/

would love any feedback

🔗 Codex-maxxing - Jason Liu

Codex-maxxing[¶](https://jxnl.github.io#codex-maxxing)
I was already using coding agents a lot before Codex. Mostly, though, I used them through interfaces built for coding work: making diffs, changing repos, and shipping code.
Around November, I started pushing them into knowledge work too. I made presentations in [Slidev](https://sli.dev/), used agents more like note-takers with voice input, and kept looking for other artifacts a coding agent could help me produce: an index.html
, a PDF, a spreadsheet, a slide deck.
The latest Codex app upgrades are the first thing I've used that make that broader mode feel native. Codex is still excellent for coding, but the more interesting shift is that it gives my work somewhere to live.
What changed my behavior was learning to give work an operating loop: a durable thread, shared memory, tools that can act on my computer, ways to steer and resume the task, and a surface where I can review the artifact itself.
Durable threads[¶](https://jxnl.github.io#durable-threads)
The first thing that changed my behavior was compaction.
I now keep a pinned thread for every important workstream I care about:
- my Chief of Staff thread
[the Agents SDK](https://openai.com/index/the-next-evolution-of-the-agents-sdk/)[the OpenAI CLI](https://github.com/openai/openai-cli)[Codex for open source](https://openai.com/form/codex-for-oss)- one just to monitor Twitter
These are not short chats. They are megathreads that I have been compacting for months. They accumulate history, preferences, and old decisions that I do not want to recreate every time I come back.
Pinned thread shortcuts
You can jump directly to pinned threads with Command-1
through Command-9
.
There is a tradeoff here. Long-running threads are not free. If you revisit them later, the conversation is probably no longer in cache, so you can incur more cost than you would in a fresh short thread. For workstreams I care about, continuity is worth it.
Voice input[¶](https://jxnl.github.io#voice-input)
Voice input gets more of my actual thinking into Codex.
The benefit is not speed. It is that the agent gets the unedited version of my thinking. Codex has built-in voice input, but I also use Wispr Flow because system-wide dictation changes how much context I can feed into everything else too. If I am planning a piece of work, I might say, "I think there is some guy named Ben in Slack who mentioned this, I do not remember exactly what, just go look." That sentence is too vague and annoying to type, but completely natural to say.
The same thing applies to transcripts. If I want to write a post, I can call someone, record the conversation, or talk to them in person with Granola on my phone, then use the transcript as the starting material. A lot of plans get better when the model has access to the messy version of what I think, not just the polished one.
Steering[¶](https://jxnl.github.io#steering)
Voice becomes more useful when combined with steering.
Steering lets you inject the next message after a tool call. If I am reviewing a website, I can keep talking while I look at it:
- make this smaller
- this copy is wrong
- the spacing between these two things feels off
- once this is done, open a PR
- wait for the preview deploy
- send the preview link to the person who needs to review it on Slack
I do not need to wait for each step to finish before deciding the next one. I can keep adding intent while the agent is still working, then walk away with the queue already shaped.
Later, Heartbeats can monitor the PR or Slack thread after I leave. The unit of work stops being "one prompt, one answer." It becomes a small operating loop.
Memory[¶](https://jxnl.github.io#memory)
Once threads started lasting longer, they needed shared memory outside any one repo.
The important move is not just preserving message history. A long thread can remember a lot, but that memory is trapped inside the thread unless the useful parts get serialized somewhere durable. The point of

🔗 Six levels of complexity in a Codex morning brief - Jason Liu

Six levels of complexity in a Codex morning brief[¶](https://jxnl.co#six-levels-of-complexity-in-a-codex-morning-brief)
This is the easiest way I know to teach someone how to use AI.
Not by starting with models, agents, or some abstract taxonomy of what the technology can do. Start with a job people already understand, then make that job quietly more powerful.
The morning brief works because almost everyone already has one. They just assemble it badly.
I think the morning brief is the first Codex workflow that normal people actually understand.
You wake up, open Slack, check your calendar, click into email, forget why you opened email, go back to Slack, then realize you have a meeting in seven minutes and no idea what happened yesterday.
The appeal is simple: help me remember what is going on.
When we were talking about Codex onboarding, this was the first workflow that felt both boring enough to teach and strong enough to matter. It starts as a dumb little orientation prompt. If you keep pushing it, it turns into a pretty good model for how people actually graduate into using Codex seriously.
Start with the thing a beginner can understand. Then add one real capability at a time until the shape of the whole system becomes obvious.
I think there are six real levels.
Level 1: ask your actual day what is going on[¶](https://jxnl.co#level-1-ask-your-actual-day-what-is-going-on)
The first version is almost embarrassingly small.
Connect Slack, Gmail, and Calendar, then ask:
Using Slack, Gmail, and Calendar, what do I have going on today?
Just see whether Codex can look across the three places your work usually hides and tell you something you actually care about.
Maybe it notices the Slack thread where someone is waiting on you. Maybe it finds the meeting you forgot to prepare for. Maybe it catches the email that changes what that meeting is even about.
If that gives you a cleaner first ten minutes of the day, it worked.
Level 2: add an agents file[¶](https://jxnl.co#level-2-add-an-agents-file)
The second level is adding a little bit of persistent instruction.
You already have enough raw surface area for Codex to be useful. Now you need to stop it from being generically helpful every single morning.
This is where an agents file becomes useful. Not as a piece of infrastructure trivia, but as a place to say how you want this work shaped by default.
For the morning brief, that might look like:
Give me a morning brief.
Focus on:
- people waiting on me
- meetings that need preparation
- commitments I made yesterday that are still open
- anything that changed overnight and affects today's priorities
Use clear headers and bullet points.
Organize the brief into:
- To-dos
- Needs replies
- Project-level updates
For anything in "Needs replies":
- include the direct Slack link
- say what the person is waiting on
- include just enough context for me to decide whether to answer now
Keep it short, structured, and easy to scan.
You do not need to worry about where the file lives. Just tell Codex:
Then paste in the instructions above. The point is to define your taste once, then let every future brief start from there.
You are not trying to sound sophisticated. You are trying to make tomorrow morning less annoying than this morning.
For other jobs, the instructions change. Recruiters might want briefs grouped by candidate. Engineers might want blockers separated from code review. Comms people might want external scans split from internal asks. But the move is the same: first give Codex the real context, then give it your defaults.
Level 3: ask it to keep an eye on this[¶](https://jxnl.co#level-3-ask-it-to-keep-an-eye-on-this)
The third level is adding recurrence, but I do not think I would teach it as "create an automation."
I would say:
Keep an eye on this every weekday morning.
That is the instruction people actually remember.
Under the hood, yes, you are turning the morning brief into a recurring automation. In practice, you are just saying: thi

The open web catalog
A browser CLI for your AI Agents
One CLI for skills, browser primitives, debugging, and cloud sessions, designed to be driven by AI Agents.
npm install -g browse
Give AI Agents the skills to automate websites from the open web catalog. Suggested DOM selectors and XHR requests cut token costs by 50x.
$ browse skills add alltrails.com
$ browse skills add recreation.gov
$ browse skills add weather.gov
$ browse skills add plugshare.com
$ browse skills add ramp.com
$ claude "Plan a road trip to Utah with EV charging stops and campsites for each night. Book and reimburse on Ramp."
Drive any page with low-level primitives: click, scroll, type, hover, press. Address elements by selector or by the AI Agent's accessibility refs.
$ browse click "input#search"
$ browse type "Apartments in SF"
$ browse select @8 "Single family unit"
$ browse press "Enter"
$ browse mouse scroll 50 50 10 10
$ browse screenshot
Tail the network and console of any browse session in real time. AI Agents (and you) see exactly what the page did.
$ browse network --tail
$ browse console --tail
GET /api/listings 200 124 ms
POST /api/filter 200 84 ms
warn deprecated: useLayoutEffect on server
error Uncaught TypeError: cannot read 'id'
All CLI commands work natively with local Chromium. Switch to remote sessions on [Browserbase's Platform](https://browserbase.run/DwFeRsP) by prefixing any command with cloud
.
# create a remote chromium session on Browserbase
$ browse cloud sessions create
# use Browserbase's Search API
$ browse cloud search "Latest White House press release"
# use Browserbase's Fetch API
$ browse cloud fetch "https://www.nytimes.com/section/us"

A browser hour goes further than you think. A typical web scrape runs in under 2 minutes. 100 hours is roughly 3,000 page-level tasks.
"It's hard to measure peace of mind. The key is that I no longer have to think about this."
"Browserbase has allowed us to abstract away the difficulties of getting data that traditionally doesn't have APIs."
"It's good to have someone reliable handling the browser management and CDN challenges so we can focus on the intelligence layer."
"The BB team has become like our in-house browser team. They handle debugging and shipping features for our browsers, so we can focus on what we do best."

[Browsers](https://www.browserbase.com/browsers): give agents complete control over fleets of headless browsers to interact with websites[Fetch and Search APIs](https://www.browserbase.com/search): agents can quickly search and fetch LLM context from the web for quick and token-efficient decisions[Agent Identity](https://www.browserbase.com/identity): enable agents to access any website with a combination of strategic partnerships (ex: Cloudflare) and a dedicated stealth research team[Runtime](https://www.browserbase.com/runtime): deploy and run agents on Browserbase for faster & more secure execution[Model Gateway](https://www.notion.so/Model-Gateway-1-Pager-2ea3c11b66148024b26df7099ebedae3?pvs=21): your Browserbase API key gives access to major models via Stagehand and unified billing.
Companies across industries use Browserbase for browser agents tasks including:
- Healthcare: Automating insurance verification, prior authorization checks, and claims processing across multiple payor portals
- Financial Services: Loan application workflows, subscription management, and regulatory compliance tasks
- Real Estate: Property listing synchronization across MLS systems, transaction processing automation, and document management
- HR & Payroll: Benefits administration, expense report processing, and employee onboarding workflows
- General Business Operations: Data entry automation, system migrations, document extraction, and web scraping
Browserbase integrates seamlessly with popular automation frameworks and AI tools:
- Automation Frameworks: Playwright, Puppeteer, Selenium, Stageh

GREG ISENBERG (@gregisenberg)

http://x.com/i/article/2056351240506974209

📄 X Article: "AI Is Eating The World" 79 slide deck from Benedict Evans

X Article full text (4,070 chars)
My favorite slides (and takeaways) from Benedict Evans "AI is Eating the World" slide deck.
Slide 4 - Tech moves in platform shifts
The amout of wealth that will be created during this platform shift is hard to even comprehend.
I remember living in Sili
As of now, the opportunities are endless for company creation.
Never let a good platform shift go to waste ;)
Slide 6 - Platform shifts reset the tech industry
Microsoft went from 95% of computing to 10% in a decade. Microsoft owned computing until the computer moved to your pocket
In a blink of an eye, it vanished. This is the cool part if you're building a company during a platform shift, the world is your oyster.
Anything is possible.
Slide 23 - Sam Altman's POV on the future
I think Sam is right that people will buy intelligence like a commodity like electricity. My best guess is they'll pick the cheapest provider that clears a quality bar, the same way you pick an electricity provider. Nobody cares who generates their power. They care that the lights turn on. That's where models are headed. Which means the value shifts entirely to what you build on top of the meter.
Slide 26 - What will equilibrium look like?
This is why I keep saying build the vertical apps. The model layer is turning into a capital-intensive commodity with low margins and no network effects. The application layer, the vertical agent that solves one problem for one industry, that's where the network effects, the margins, and the monopolies re-form. The value is moving up the stack. Build there.
The margin lives with the customer relationship and data.
Slide 27 - Thesis on AI
Chat is terrible UX. Agreed. The labs can't build all the apps. Obviously. Models are commodities with no network effects. Already happening. Which means: innovation moves up the stack. Straight to the founders building real products for real industries on top of commodity intelligence.
That's good news for us who want to build.
Slide 30 - Consumer use is a mile wide and an inch deep
Everyone talks about AI adoption like it's universal (esp on X). This chart says otherwise. Most people use ChatGPT the way they use a calculator. Occasionally. When they remember it exists. The founders who win consumer AI will make products people use daily without realizing they're "using AI."
Slide 37 - ChatGPT product/market fit
Look at those tiny bars. Legal, support, medical, real estate, finance. Every single one of those is a massive industry spending almost nothing on AI right now. Coding got to $3B because developers adopted first. Every other category is still at the starting line. That's the whole opportunity map in one chart.
Now just go find the sub-niches/vertical use-cases that heavily funded VC companies aren't going after already.
Dare I say... we are so early?
Slide 48 - Startups exist to unbundle use cases
YC gets it. Looks like 85% of its latest batches are AI pilled.
The unbundling of software has begun.
The rush is here.
Slide 54 - Sometimes a job is just a task to be automated
Elevators won't replace us, people who know how to use elevators will?
Elevator attendants were a big contributor to society and then vanished.
History doesn't repeat itself but it certainly rhymes.
Slide 61 - What was impossible that now become cheap?
Benedict is asking the right questions:
What if you had a million interns?
What if you had one intern who was a million times faster?
My big question here is... what businesses does this unlock?
Slide 74 - no one knows anything
The only thing we know is experimenting is the way to do it. Come up with your own ideas, or grab one from Ideabrowser
Whatever you do, experimenting a lot is key during platform shifts.
It'll take you experimenting on a few ideas to get to the right one.
And yeah, no one truly knows anything.
The only way out is through.
This is the most incredible time to be building.
Reading through this deck definitely reminded me of that. You can read the full deck here.
Happy building.
I'm rooting for you,
Greg Isenberg
gregisenberg.com

item.content:encoded:
Hiten Shah (@hnshah)

http://x.com/i/article/2056250841905201152

📄 X Article: The new startup bottleneck

X Article full text (6,624 chars)
Founders are shipping so much right now that a lot of them have lost the thread. A demo works. Launch goes out. Teams feel momentum. Then the uncomfortable part shows up. Nobody knows what the company learned.
That is the part of this AI moment I cannot stop thinking about.
It came up in my conversation with Luba because she asked what has changed for founders. My answer keeps getting simpler the more I think about it.
We can build more.
Learning has not caught up.
Back in the day, I learned Lean Startup from Eric Ries and Sean Ellis. Eric gave the world build, measure, learn. Sean made the learning part feel real to me because he came at it through growth. He cared about the loop getting tighter. Put something into the world. See what happened. Learn from it. Go around again.
That still sounds basic.
It is still the whole game.
AI changed the emotional weight of building.
A small team can make a prototype in the morning. One founder can turn a rough thought into a working demo. Product people can explore five directions where they used to explore one. Engineers have tools that take a lot of the blank-page pain out of implementation.
Useful stuff.
Also dangerous.
Motion has a drug-like quality for founders. You had an idea. Now it exists. The team can see it. Customers can click it. Investors can react to it. Social can screenshot it.
For a minute, that feels like progress.
Then comes the part most teams are not set up for.
Did it matter?
Who used it?
Why did they care?
Where did they get stuck?
What did it teach us that changes what we do next?
Those questions are slower than the demo. They are also where the company gets smarter.
I think this is why so many founders feel a weird mix of excitement and anxiety right now. They are moving faster. Their product is changing more often. The roadmap has more options. Everything looks more alive.
Clarity is not increasing at the same rate.
That gap is the bottleneck.
Learning capacity.
A company can now create more product surface area than it can understand. That sounds like a good problem until you live with it. Every new feature asks for a relationship with the company. Customers have to understand it. Support has to explain it. Product has to remember why it exists. Engineering has to maintain it. Someone has to decide when it should die.
Shipping is a moment.
Learning is a system.
You can feel the difference as a user.
Some products feel like the team learned before they shipped. The use case is clear. Edges make sense. You can tell someone cared about the path from first click to value.
Other products feel like the team shipped so they could find out what they were building.
That can work for a prototype.
It gets expensive as a habit.
The example I brought up with Luba was Gamma. Grant Lee talked with Lenny about their process, and what stuck with me was how completely they compress the loop.
Idea in the morning.
Functional prototype.
Real prospective users who do not care if Gamma succeeds.
Experiment in the afternoon.
Watch people struggle.
Review what happened by evening or the next day.
That is speed with a brain attached.
The prototype creates contact with reality. User testing shows where the idea breaks. Review turns pain into a decision.
A lot of teams stop at the artifact.
Strong teams finish the loop.
That is the distinction I think people are missing in the AI conversation. Everyone keeps asking how fast they can ship. A more useful question is how fast the company can learn from what it ships.
Very different muscles.
Shipping fast takes tools and urgency.
Learning fast takes taste, customer access, instrumentation, decision cadence, and enough humility to hear what the market just told you.
Many companies are training the first muscle hard right now.
The second one is undertrained.
That creates a feeling founders know well. Busy team. Changing product. Full roadmap. Lots of energy. Somehow the company does not feel sharper.
Usually, that means unresolved learning is piling up.
Why did one segment use the feature and another ignore it?
Which customer problem did the launch actually solve?
Where did the product get harder to explain?
What got built because AI made it easy?
Which idea earned another week?
What needs to die quietly before it becomes permanent?
These questions kill the high of shipping.
They also make the company better.
Before AI, engineering capacity forced some discipline. Teams had to choose. Waiting was part of the process. Prioritization had teeth because every yes cost real time.
AI removes some of that friction.
So the discipline has to come from the founder.
Product judgment matters more now. Customer understanding matters more. Taste matters more. Knowing what kind of company you are building matters more.
That last one is where a lot of founders get stuck.
Luba and I also talked about the lost craft of startups. I see this a lot with first-time founders. Basics I assumed were already codified are missing. Sometimes I send someone a doc and say, just do this. Skip the 15 conversations. Forget the consultant for now. Try this exact thing and see what happens.
Someone once joked that I had a secret document network.
None of it is secret.
It is craft.
Tech became an industry. Some of the craft got buried under content, capital, speed, hype, playbooks, founder mythology, and a lot of advice from people who have not done the work.
AI is going to expose that.
A founder with craft can use AI to tighten the learning loop.
Without that craft, AI can create a larger mess at a faster pace.
You see the difference after shipping.
One team asks what else can we build.
Another asks what do we know now.
That second question is where the leverage is.
At Crazy Egg, we are pushing ourselves to ship something meaningful every month. I would love to get that cadence even faster. The part I care about most is whether the shipping is tied to learning.
We heard something.
Customers showed us something.
Our understanding changed.
Then we shipped because of it.
That is the kind of speed I trust.
AI gives founders more shots on goal.
More shots help only when you get better at aiming.
The best companies in this cycle will ship fast because the market demands it. They will learn faster because that is how speed compounds.
Product activity is the visible part.
What you want is a company that gets smarter every time it ships.
I talked about this with Luba in our full conversation here https://youtu.be/_nX16BHnDbo
The two parts that connect most to this essay
Build fast and learn fast
The lost craft of startups https://youtu.be/_nX16BHnDbo?t=4891

It came up in my conversation with Luba because she asked what has changed for founders. My answer keeps getting simpler the more I think about it.
We can build more.
Learning has not caught up.
Back in the day, I learned Lean Startup from Eric Ries and Sean Ellis. Eric gave the world build, measure, learn. Sean made the learning part feel real to me because he came at it through growth. He cared about the loop getting tighter. Put something into the world. See what happened. Learn from it. Go around again.
That still sounds basic.
It is still the whole game.
AI changed the emotional weight of building.
A small team can make a prototype in the morning. One founder can turn a rough thought into a working demo. Product people can explore five directions where they used to explore one. Engineers have tools that take a lot of the blank-page pain out of implementation.
Useful stuff.
Also dangerous.
Motion has a drug-like quality for founders. You had an idea. Now it exists. The team can see it. Customers can click it. Investors can react to it. Social can screenshot it.
For a minute, that feels like progress.
Then comes the part most teams are not set up for.
Did it matter?
Who used it?
Why did they care?
Where did they get stuck?
What did it teach us that changes what we do next?
Those questions are slower than the demo. They are also where the company gets smarter.
I think this is why so many founders feel a weird mix of excitement and anxiety right now. They are moving faster. Their product is changing more often. The roadmap has more options. Everything looks more alive.
Clarity is not increasing at the same rate.
That gap is the bottleneck.
Learning capacity.
A company can now create more product surface area than it can understand. That sounds like a good problem until you live with it. Every new feature asks for a relationship with the company. Customers have to understand it. Support has to explain it. Product has to remember why it exists. Engineering has to maintain it. Someone has to decide when it should die.
Shipping is a moment.
Learning is a system.
You can feel the difference as a user.
Some products feel like the team learned before they shipped. The use case is clear. Edges make sense. You can tell someone cared about the path from first click to value.
Other products feel like the team shipped so they could find out what they were building.
That can work for a prototype.
It gets expensive as a habit.
The example I brought up with Luba was Gamma. Grant Lee talked with Lenny about their process, and what stuck with me was how completely they compress the loop.
Idea in the morning.
Functional prototype.
Real prospective users who do not care if Gamma succeeds.
Experiment in the afternoon.
Watch people struggle.
Review what happened by evening or the next day.
Tha

📄 X Article: Measuring the Delegation Intelligence of Agents

X Article full text (15,485 chars)
From "can the model do it?" to "does the model know how to do it?"
2026 is almost half over. Looking back, the biggest shift this year is that the Agent paradigm finally moved from demo to production. From Auto Research to long-horizon coding, from OS-level operations to multi-tool orchestration, model capability has been reassembled:
Agent = Model + Harness
has become the default engineering paradigm for almost everyone.
I've spent the past few years doing evaluation work (FairEval, Video-MME etc.) and model training (MiMo and Reka), and the past year specifically deep in the trenches of Agent evaluation.
The more I do it, the more I feel: this field is going through a paradigm shift, and most of us are still measuring new things with old rulers.
So I'm putting these thoughts into writing. This isn't a survey — it's a position piece, shaped by the bruises and iterations of building things. Most of the methods I'll unpack below come from Claw-Eval, the Agent evaluation framework our team built.
If you do eval, I hope this helps. If you build agents or models, I hope it helps you see what the numbers on a leaderboard are actually pointing at.
1. What Makes a Good Eval?
A good evaluation, in my mind, does three things at once.
First, it maps the boundary of model capability. A good benchmark isn't a thermometer that spits out a number — it's a map that tells you *where* a model works and *where* it breaks.
Second, it advances evaluation methodology itself. LLM-as-a-judge, finer-grained step-level scoring, structured analysis of trajectories — these methodological improvements often outlast any single benchmark's relevance.
Third, it opens up new imagination. This one is the most underrated.
Case in point: OSWorld and SWE-Bench were among the best things the previous era produced. OSWorld pushed evaluation from single-turn QA to real operating system tasks. SWE-Bench saw the coding explosion coming early and set the standard for software engineering evaluation. They moved the frame from "answer this question" to "operate in an environment with real side effects." The impact went far beyond adding another benchmark to the pile — they **retroactively defined what model capability could even mean.**
Recently, ProgramBench and RepoZero pushed that imagination further with long-horizon coding tasks that require cross-file, cross-module changes in real codebases. Not completing a function — navigating a codebase with history. And as AutoResearch emerged, evaluation followed, letting us measure open-ended, long-range research tasks.
Good evals don't just measure capability. They define what capability is worth pursuing.
2. The Ceiling of Traditional Benchmarks Is Caving In
Let me be direct: a lot of capability evaluations we used to be proud of are losing relevance at visible speed.
The awkwardness of knowledge benchmarks
Models don't need to memorize Wikipedia. When web search is a standard tool in the harness, real-time, post-cutoff knowledge is always one query away. Grinding out higher scores on knowledge QA is increasingly about patching the long tail — and the ROI on that tail keeps dropping.
The awkwardness of long-chain reasoning benchmarks
Rubik's cube state tracking, dice-roll probability chains, complex combinatorics — the "prestige" of these problems is eroding under the Agent paradigm. The reason is simple: five lines of Python Monte Carlo are more reliable than a 20-step mental chain. A model with access to a code interpreter doesn't succeed on these problems because of its "reasoning depth" — it succeeds because it realizes this should be done in code.
The harness, in many scenarios, sidesteps the stochastic brittleness of long reasoning chains. When we see scores climbing on these benchmarks, we need to ask: are we measuring capability, or are we measuring "used the right tool"?
A necessary boundary condition
The argument above holds only when base capabilities are sufficient.
I'm not saying base capability evaluation doesn't matter. When models haven't broadly hit frontier scale, or when you're working on small models or specialized verticals, base eval is still the most reliable gap-finding tool — that's a principle. What I'm flagging is this: when your target model is already at the frontier, pouring massive resources into base capability benchmarks might mean patching an extremely long tail that distillation or data synthesis will catch up to anyway.
Over the medium term, base capabilities trickle down from large models to small ones, which makes this divergence less and less meaningful.
So the question isn't "should we still measure base capabilities."
It's "where should the main evaluation battlefield be for frontier models?"
3. What Should We Actually Measure? Delegation Intelligence, Maybe
Now for the constructive half.
After discussing this with Claude and GPT, I think the right name is Delegation Intelligence.
The core argument is simple: we need to measure not whether a model can do something, but whether it knows how to get it done.
Here's an analogy. A good engineer doesn't mentally compute 2^37 × 1.0732 — they open a calculator. Their "intelligence" isn't about handling giant numbers in their head. It's about **knowing this task should be delegated to a calculator.** Similarly, a truly capable model doesn't need every ability internalized in its weights. It needs to know: when to reason directly, when to invoke a tool, when to search, when to run code, and when to pause and cross-verify.
Delegation Intelligence, as I see it, has at least three dimensions:
Tool use judgment: knowing when to use a tool, which tool to use, and with what parameters
Information synthesis & verification: integrating multi-source information and assessing source reliability
Path selection: choosing between direct reasoning, code execution, and web search
Three examples to build intuition.
Example 1: knowledge delegation
**Question**: "What was Company X's Q1 2026 revenue?"
Model A draws from training memory and confidently gives a 2024 figure. Model B immediately recognizes this requires current information, invokes web search, cross-verifies across two independent sources, and returns the answer with source attribution and timestamps.
Which is smarter? Model B, obviously. B's self-awareness beats A's breadth of memory.
Example 2: computational delegation
**Question**: "If you roll a standard die 10 times, what's the probability of at least one back-to-back pair of sixes?"
Model A computes conditional probabilities by hand — long chain, one mistake and it's all wrong. Model B writes five lines of Python Monte Carlo, runs 100k simulations, gets a stable answer, and optionally provides a 95% confidence interval.
B doesn't have a "smarter brain." It has **smarter judgment.**
Example 3: information weighting
**Question**: "Is drug X effective for condition Y?"
The search returns three sources: an RCT in *Nature*, a personal blog post, and a 2018 outdated review. Model A evenly averages all sources and produces a vague "possibly effective." Model B prioritizes the RCT, flags the blog as low-weight with reasoning, notes the review's temporal limitations, and delivers a structured, confidence-calibrated answer.
This is the core of information synthesis, weighting, not averaging.
Circling back to Part 1: the benchmarks that mattered are important precisely because these are tasks you can't brute-force with "raw brainpower." They only get solved through delegation intelligence. "Imaginative scenarios" and "what's worth measuring" are the same loop.
4. Claw-Eval in Practice: How We Measure Delegation Intelligence
Theory sounds nice, but without metrics it's just a slogan. This section is about what we actually do in Claw-Eval.
Two dimensions: outcome + path
Final answers alone aren't enough. Agent evaluation has to track both:
Outcome correctness: design tasks with verifiable answers — unit tests, numeric results, file diffs, API states. If a machine can verify it, don't use an LLM judge. If an LLM judge works, don't use humans.
Path soundness: record all tool calls and use the trajectory as an audit surface. Crucially: acknowledge that there are many valid paths. Two agents might solve the same task — one via search + synthesis, another via code + verification. If the path is reasonable and the result is correct, both should count. Forcing a single prescribed path undermines evaluation fairness.
From Pass@k to Pass-all-k
Pass@k measures "at least 1 success in k attempts" — the dominant metric of recent years. In Agent evaluation, we increasingly lean on **Pass-all-k**: **every one of k attempts succeeds.**
The interesting thing is the **gap**:
\text{Stability Gap} = \text{Pass@}k - \text{Pass-all-}k
Large gap: the model gets lucky — sometimes it works, but the path isn't stable
Small gap: the decision path is stable and converging
Only when the gap is small enough do I consider a model's Delegation Intelligence truly there. Stability itself is a signal of judgment. A model that picks the wrong tool or skips a verification step because of random perturbation isn't a model that "knows how to do it."
People also ask: why build our own harness instead of using something like OpenClaw? The answer is better auditability.
And a more general answer: treat harness adaptability as an independent evaluation dimension.A truly strong model should maintain stable performance across different prompt templates, tool sets, and execution environments. In future Claw-Eval runs, we'll test the same model across multiple harness configurations and look at score variance — adaptability is itself a generalization metric.
Cost-aware metrics: Token Efficiency
Getting it right isn't enough — we need to know *what it cost* to get there.
Claw-Eval also tracks token efficiency: can the model arrive at the correct answer with the fewest possible tool calls, the shortest trajectory, the least token spend? In production this is directly tied to cost. In evaluation, it reflects the model's "economic judgment" — a model that spends 50k tokens and a model that spends 5k tokens on the same task should not be treated equivalently.
Our leaderboard shows cost-accuracy scatter plots. Many models cluster around similar accuracy but diverge by multiples on token cost. This weighting depends on task criticality, of course — in high-stakes domains like medicine or finance, correctness far outweighs cost. That trade-off is itself a dimension evaluation design should account for.
A dimension we're starting to measure: model "instinct"
This is the part I find most compelling.
Analyzing the trajectories from agents, we've noticed something striking: **different models have wildly different "instinct," and no mainstream benchmark currently measures this.**
What do I mean? A few examples:
Some agents, without fully reading a paper, pinpoint the two key paragraphs in the method section
Some agents, without deeply knowing a codebase, glance at the directory structure and tell you which files are core and what patterns are worth grepping
Some agents with clearly insufficient information, produce first judgments that are already close to the final answer — while others need to exhaust the entire search/read loop before converging to the same conclusion
If tool use and path selection are delegation intelligence's "observable behavior," instinct is its "latent pre-computation": it explains why some models don't need to try every path — they just walk the right one from the start. This is delegation at a higher level: not "knowing how to find the answer," but "roughly knowing where the answer is before you've finished looking."
It's not the same as accuracy, and not the same as token efficiency. Two models with identical accuracy can have vastly different instinct — one tried every path until it stumbled on the right one, the other walked straight there. The final score may not show the difference, but the trajectory makes it obvious. Token efficiency is a partial proxy but doesn't fully capture it.
These are early observations. But I'm increasingly convinced: whoever figures out how to define and measure "model instinct" is drawing the capability map for the next era.
5. The Severely Underrated Engineering Challenges
Now for some things that aren't "intellectual" but drastically affect whether your evaluation results are trustworthy. This is where the Claw-Eval team has bled the most.
I'll split these into two groups.
Infrastructure-side problems
Model service stability: at evaluation scale, sporadic endpoint timeouts, rate limiting, context window truncation — all of these contaminate results. A full eval run might take dozens of hours. One hiccup in the middle can make you question everything.
Harness service stability: Agent evaluation is far more environment-sensitive than QA evaluation. Browser automation freezes, shell containers crash, filesystem state drifts — none of these are "model problems," but they get attributed to the model.
Docker resource adequacy: for computation-heavy tasks, CPU, memory, and disk quotas must be sufficient. **Isolation isn't just about environment isolation — it's about resource isolation.** One OOM task can bring down the entire evaluation pipeline.
Evaluation design problems
Model-harness mismatch: the same model under different system prompts can differ by 20 points. **Mismatch severely undermines cross-model comparability.** This is exactly why we emphasize measuring adaptability as a standalone dimension.
Mock service volatility: web search is one of the trickiest tools in evaluation. The same query returns different results today versus tomorrow — this makes "ground truth" drift. Either use snapshots, or design tasks that avoid strong time-sensitivity.
A dimension that doesn't get enough attention: safety
When agents can invoke tools autonomously, evaluation should naturally include one more dimension: does the model invoke tools it shouldn't, delete files it shouldn't, or leak information it shouldn't?
The community hasn't discussed this enough, but when an agent can operate on a filesystem and make network requests, "staying within boundaries" matters as much as "being clever."
In Claw-Eval, we design trap tasks to observe these behaviors, and safety violations carry a one-strike veto in scoring — reflecting the weight safety deserves.
In Closing: The Next Station for Eval
Returning to the three criteria from the start: map capability boundaries, advance evaluation methodology, and open up new imagination. In the Agent era, all three need reinterpretation.
If you build Agent evals: prioritize delegation intelligence, look at Pass-all-k not just Pass@k, treat token efficiency as a first-class metric, and start thinking about how to measure "model instinct."
If you build base capability evals: they remain irreplaceable for small models, vertical domains, and gap detection — just be clear about whether the gap you're patching is in the long tail.
If you build models: the strong model of the Agent era isn't the one that knows everything. It's the one that knows what to do when. Delegation beats memorization.
Many of the ideas in this piece were shaped through discussions with teammates and community friends, inevitably incomplete. Agent evaluation is still a very early field. What I've written may not be right, but I hope it offers something useful to those exploring in this direction.

[Video-MME ](https://github.com/MME-Benchmarks/Video-MME)
etc.) and model training (
[Xiaomi MiMo](https://huggingface.co/XiaomiMiMo/)
and
[Reka](https://reka.ai/)
), and the past year specifically deep in the trenches of Agent evaluation.
The more I do it, the more I feel: this field is going through a paradigm shift, and most of us are still measuring new things with old rulers.
So I'm putting these thoughts into writing. This isn't a survey — it's a position piece, shaped by the bruises and iterations of building things. Most of the methods I'll unpack below come from
[Claw-Eval](https://claw-eval.github.io/)
, the Agent evaluation framework our team built.
If you do eval, I hope this helps. If you build agents or models, I hope it helps you see what the numbers on a leaderboard are actually pointing at.
##
1\. What Makes a Good Eval?
A good evaluation, in my mind, does three things at once.
First, it maps the boundary of model capability. A good benchmark isn't a thermometer that spits out a number — it's a map that tells you \*where\* a model works and \*where\* it breaks.
Second, it advances evaluation methodology itself. LLM-as-a-judge, finer-grained step-level scoring, structured analysis of trajectories — these methodological improvements often outlast any single benchmark's relevance.
Third, it opens up new imagination. This one is the most underrated.
Case in point:
[ OSWorld ](https://os-world.github.io/)
and
[SWE-Bench](https://www.swebench.com/)
were among the best things the previous era produced. OSWorld pushed evaluation from single-turn QA to real operating system tasks. SWE-Bench saw the coding explosion coming early and set the standard for software engineering evaluation. They moved the frame from "answer this question" to "operate in an environment with real side effects." The impact went far beyond adding another benchmark to the pile — they \*\*retroactively defined what model capability could even mean.\*\*
Recently,
[ProgramBench](https://programbench.com/)
and
[RepoZero](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07122)
pushed that imagination further with long-horizon coding tasks that require cross-file, cross-module changes in real codebases. Not completing a function — navigating a codebase with history. And as
[AutoResearch](https://github.com/karpathy/autoresearch)
emerged, evaluation followed, letting us measure open-ended, long-range research tasks.
Good evals don't just measure capability. They define what capability is worth pursuing.
##
2\. The Ceiling of Traditional Benchmarks Is Caving In
Let me be direct: a lot of capability evaluations we used to be proud of are losing

item.content:encoded:
Addy Osmani (@addyosmani)

http://x.com/i/article/2055936913211899904

📄 X Article: Don't Outsource the Learning

X Article full text (7,934 chars)
Right now, it's too easy to let AI write the code while you skip the learning. The bug gets fixed but your mental model doesn't move. We are silently trading future capability for present-day speed, and the tools won't force us to do otherwise. That part has to come from you.
There's a default loop most of us have settled into. You paste in a spec or error message. The model hands you a fix. The symptom vanishes. You ship. Somewhere in that loop, the messy struggle between problem and solution stops happening at all.
I've written before about cognitive surrender, the moment an AI reviewer's verdict quietly replaces your own. This is the solo version of that same loop. It's just you and the model. The model is faster, so you stop trying to compete on comprehension. Across thousands of these small interactions, what you can actually build without an AI looking over your shoulder gets a little weaker every week. None of these moments feel like a problem on the day they happen.
I'm not anti-AI. I use these tools daily and have shipped more with them in the last year than in the years before it. But the default way we use them is optimized for one thing: closing tasks. That is a completely different goal from staying sharp enough to steer them over a career that spans a long time.
The studies are converging on the same point
Several pieces of research over the last year have landed in roughly the same place.
Anthropic ran a randomized trial in early 2026 where engineers learned a new Python library, half with AI assistance and half without. Both groups finished the tasks at the same speed. But the AI group bombed the follow-up comprehension quiz: 50% versus 67% for the manual group, with the gap widening on debugging. The interesting cut was inside the AI group itself. Engineers who used AI to ask conceptual questions scored above 65%. Engineers who copy-pasted the generated code scored under 40%. The tool didn't determine the outcome. The posture did.
MIT's Your Brain on ChatGPT study compared essay writing across LLM, search-engine, and brain-only groups. EEG measurements showed brain connectivity scaling down with every layer of external support. The LLM group showed the weakest coupling. After writing the essay, 83% of LLM users couldn't quote a single line of what they had just produced. The researchers called this cognitive debt: saving mental effort today, paying for it in critical thinking tomorrow.
A CHI 2026 study added a related finding. When people had LLM access at the start of a task, the LLM framed the entire problem. Even when the human did the rest of the work themselves, that initial anchoring produced measurably worse decisions. The order of operations mattered more than the total amount of AI used.
Different methodologies reaching the same conclusion. Using AI without an active intent to learn quietly degrades the skill you're being paid for.
The tools default to shipping, not teaching
If you fire up a coding agent and stick to the defaults, everything is tuned for one metric: getting the task done.
The model writes the code. You accept it. The loop repeats. At no point does the tool pause and ask "what do you think the problem is?" or "try writing the first five lines yourself."
That's where UX gravity is right now. Product teams get rewarded for merged changes and shorter cycle times, not for making you a sharper engineer. We all want fewer keystrokes, so the tools have sanded the friction away. The trouble is that friction was where the learning lived.
A few companies have tried pushing back.
Anthropic shipped Learning Mode for Claude, which uses Socratic questioning and stops to ask you to write code before continuing. OpenAI and Google have shipped similar features. Almost nobody uses them for real production work though if we're being real. We've quietly filed them under "for students" and that's a mistake. The same feature that helps a sophomore learn React works for a senior engineer learning Rust. You just have to be willing to feel like a beginner again.
"If the AI can do it, why do I need to understand it?"
A fair question. For some work, the answer is: you don't. If it's boilerplate, glue code, or a throwaway CI script you'll never look at again, delegate it. The opportunity cost of memorizing YAML syntax is too high.
For real software, pure delegation breaks down in a few specific places.
When something breaks. AI-generated code crashes the same way human code does. "The agent wrote it" doesn't help you debug problems. Somebody on the team has to understand the architecture.
When it's confidently wrong. LLMs hallucinate. The only defense against a plausible-looking incorrect answer is enough expertise to spot it.
When the foundation changes. Code is temporary; systems are permanent. When frameworks update or a security review flags a structural issue, you can't re-prompt your way out. You need engineers who understand the system well enough to migrate it.
When you leave the median. AI is brilliant at problems that have been solved a million times on GitHub. The further you stray from the median, the worse it gets. The hard, undocumented problems, the ones that justify a senior engineer's salary, still require deep understanding.
When the market adjusts. That 20% drop in junior developer employment since 2022 isn't a fluke. Engineers who can only ship with AI, and not without it, are entering a labor pool that is already re-pricing what expertise is worth.
If you use AI to skip learning, you're trading future relevance for a slightly easier Tuesday.
The fix is in how you prompt, not whether you do
The good news is that the same tools that produce cognitive debt can produce sharper engineers. The difference is in what you ask of them.
Form a hypothesis before you ask. Before requesting a fix, write down two or three sentences on what you think the problem is. Use the model's answer to test your theory, not to replace it.
Ask for the explanation before the code. In unfamiliar territory, your first prompt should be something like "explain how this works, what the alternatives are, and what the tradeoffs are." Ask for the code only after you've grasped the concepts.
Turn on Learning Mode when you're out of your depth. Claude has it. ChatGPT has Study Mode. Gemini has Guided Learning. Yes, it feels slower. That's the point.
Treat AI output like a PR from a junior engineer. Read it. Critique it. Push back on it. Would you merge it just because the tests passed? If not, don't merge it here either.
Re-derive things by hand once in a while. Take a piece of code the model wrote for you and try to recreate it from scratch. It's the calibration check that tells you how much you've quietly lost.
Ask the model to teach you what it just did. After it writes a clever function, ask what concepts it used and what you'd need to read to understand the design choice. One extra prompt changes what you take away from the session.
None of these are dramatic. They're small posture shifts inside the same tools you're already using.
Two metrics, not one
I've started ending coding sessions with a simple question: did I learn anything today, or did I just close tickets?
Sometimes the honest answer is "I just closed issues" and that's fine. If it becomes the answer for months in a row, cognitive debt is accumulating in the background.
Ship and learn are two separate metrics. Your manager and your customers will only ever ask about the first one. The second is on you.
I'd rather ship 80% of what I could have and learn 100% of what I needed to, than the reverse. Over years, those two strategies produce very different engineers.
You don't have to choose between using AI and learning. You do have to choose a workflow that does both, because the defaults won't choose it for you. The tools are ready whenever you are.
The next boring task you were about to delegate is a good place to start.

item.title: @Xudong07452910: 为什么AI 时代，别追网红，要追 Builder
item.dc:creator: Xudong Han
item.description:
http://x.com/i/article/2055613452798902272
Tweet: https://x.com/Xudong07452910/status/2055904097358794948 X article: https://x.com/Xudong07452910/article/2055904097358794948 X article text: 选择关注谁，决定你会成为什么。 最近这一年，我越来越明显地感觉到一件事：很多人每天都在高强度「关注 AI」，但真正开始动手做东西的人，其实并不多。 每天打开 X、小红书、YouTube，你都会看到大量关于 AI 的内容。有人分析行业趋势，有人预测未来职业，有人讨论 Agent 会如何改变世界，也有人不断强调「普通人最后的机会来了」。 这些内容本身并没有问题。很多人讲得确实好，逻辑清晰，表达有感染力，也帮助了不少人第一次接触 AI。 但看久了之后，你会慢慢产生一种奇怪的感觉：你好像知道了很多东西，却又什么都没有真正开始。 你收藏了几十篇「AI 创业指南」，关注了一堆「未来趋势」博主，也记住了大量热门词汇——MCP、Agent、Workflow、RAG、Multi-Agent。可回头看时会发现，自己真正做过的事情其实很少。 这种状态我自己也经历过。有段时间，我每天刷大量 AI 内容，今天有人说「AI 将淘汰程序员」，明天有人说「一个人公司时代来了」，后天又有人说「未来属于超级个体」。每句话都让人产生「再不行动就晚了」的紧迫感，可真正让我开始改变的，并不是那些宏大的观点，而是后来我越来越多地开始关注一些真正下场做事的人。 一、网红讲趋势，Builder 讲怎么做 网红的价值一直存在。他们擅长总结趋势、提炼观点、放大情绪，能让更多人第一次理解 AI 到底意味着什么。 但大部分趋势内容有一个共同特点：它们更像一种「认知消费品」。你看的时候很兴奋，觉得自己已经理解了这个时代，但这种理解往往停留在观点层面，不会真正转化成行动。 比如有人会不断告诉你：「未来一定属于 Agent」「AI 会重构所有行业」「不会用 AI 的人会被淘汰」。这些话可能都没错，但对于真正想做事的人来说，他更关心的问题是：Agent 到底解决了什么真实需求？用户为什么愿意付费？什么场景是真的高频？一个普通人应该从哪里开始？ 这些问题，往往只有真正做过产品的人才会聊。因为它们不是观点，而是经验。经验这种东西通常不够「性感」，甚至有点狼狈，但恰恰最接近真实世界。 二、Builder 的分享，会让你第一次认真想「怎么做」 我现在越来越喜欢看独立开发者的分享，原因很简单：他们讲的东西通常格外具体。 前段时间我看到一个开发者分享，说他最开始做 AI 产品时，一直以为用户最需要「AI 帮忙生成内容」，于是花了很多时间做 AI 写作、AI 总结之类的功能，技术做得不差，但用户始终不愿意付费。后来他偶然接触到一些跨境电商卖家，发现这些人每天都在重复做一件枯燥的事：整理 SKU、填写产品信息、同步平台数据。于是他花了一个周末，做了一个帮卖家自动整理商品表格的小工具。界面不漂亮，功能也不复杂，但上线后很快就有了付费用户。 这个例子让我印象极深。因为它说明真实市场和想象中的市场完全不一样——很多付费需求，不过是帮别人节省一点时间，减少一点重复劳动。 类似的还有一个人的经历：他最开始迷恋「做大产品」，想做平台、做生态、做所有人都会用的 AI 应用。折腾了大半年，功能越来越多，系统越来越复杂，但始终没人真正留下来。最后反而靠一个很小的功能活了下来：帮用户自动把会议录音整理成客户沟通纪要。这功能一点都不酷，也没有什么「AGI 感」，但因为它解决的是企业里每天都会出现的真实问题，用户愿意长期付费。 还有一种内容我现在尤其珍惜：那些坦率承认失败的分享。有人花了两个月做产品，发现根本没人用，决定关掉；有人认真复盘为什么广告投放毫无效果，为什么自以为很重要的功能用户根本不在意。 这种分享在互联网上很少见，因为大家更偏爱成功故事——「上线即爆火」「一个人三个月 ARR Xudong Han (@Xudong07452910)

📄 X Article: 为什么AI 时代，别追网红，要追 Builder

X Article full text (2,869 chars)
选择关注谁，决定你会成为什么。
最近这一年，我越来越明显地感觉到一件事：很多人每天都在高强度「关注 AI」，但真正开始动手做东西的人，其实并不多。
每天打开 X、小红书、YouTube，你都会看到大量关于 AI 的内容。有人分析行业趋势，有人预测未来职业，有人讨论 Agent 会如何改变世界，也有人不断强调「普通人最后的机会来了」。
这些内容本身并没有问题。很多人讲得确实好，逻辑清晰，表达有感染力，也帮助了不少人第一次接触 AI。
但看久了之后，你会慢慢产生一种奇怪的感觉：你好像知道了很多东西，却又什么都没有真正开始。
你收藏了几十篇「AI 创业指南」，关注了一堆「未来趋势」博主，也记住了大量热门词汇——MCP、Agent、Workflow、RAG、Multi-Agent。可回头看时会发现，自己真正做过的事情其实很少。
这种状态我自己也经历过。有段时间，我每天刷大量 AI 内容，今天有人说「AI 将淘汰程序员」，明天有人说「一个人公司时代来了」，后天又有人说「未来属于超级个体」。每句话都让人产生「再不行动就晚了」的紧迫感，可真正让我开始改变的，并不是那些宏大的观点，而是后来我越来越多地开始关注一些真正下场做事的人。
一、网红讲趋势，Builder 讲怎么做
网红的价值一直存在。他们擅长总结趋势、提炼观点、放大情绪，能让更多人第一次理解 AI 到底意味着什么。
但大部分趋势内容有一个共同特点：它们更像一种「认知消费品」。你看的时候很兴奋，觉得自己已经理解了这个时代，但这种理解往往停留在观点层面，不会真正转化成行动。
比如有人会不断告诉你：「未来一定属于 Agent」「AI 会重构所有行业」「不会用 AI 的人会被淘汰」。这些话可能都没错，但对于真正想做事的人来说，他更关心的问题是：Agent 到底解决了什么真实需求？用户为什么愿意付费？什么场景是真的高频？一个普通人应该从哪里开始？
这些问题，往往只有真正做过产品的人才会聊。因为它们不是观点，而是经验。经验这种东西通常不够「性感」，甚至有点狼狈，但恰恰最接近真实世界。
二、Builder 的分享，会让你第一次认真想「怎么做」
我现在越来越喜欢看独立开发者的分享，原因很简单：他们讲的东西通常格外具体。
前段时间我看到一个开发者分享，说他最开始做 AI 产品时，一直以为用户最需要「AI 帮忙生成内容」，于是花了很多时间做 AI 写作、AI 总结之类的功能，技术做得不差，但用户始终不愿意付费。后来他偶然接触到一些跨境电商卖家，发现这些人每天都在重复做一件枯燥的事：整理 SKU、填写产品信息、同步平台数据。于是他花了一个周末，做了一个帮卖家自动整理商品表格的小工具。界面不漂亮，功能也不复杂，但上线后很快就有了付费用户。
这个例子让我印象极深。因为它说明真实市场和想象中的市场完全不一样——很多付费需求，不过是帮别人节省一点时间，减少一点重复劳动。
类似的还有一个人的经历：他最开始迷恋「做大产品」，想做平台、做生态、做所有人都会用的 AI 应用。折腾了大半年，功能越来越多，系统越来越复杂，但始终没人真正留下来。最后反而靠一个很小的功能活了下来：帮用户自动把会议录音整理成客户沟通纪要。这功能一点都不酷，也没有什么「AGI 感」，但因为它解决的是企业里每天都会出现的真实问题，用户愿意长期付费。
还有一种内容我现在尤其珍惜：那些坦率承认失败的分享。有人花了两个月做产品，发现根本没人用，决定关掉；有人认真复盘为什么广告投放毫无效果，为什么自以为很重要的功能用户根本不在意。
这种分享在互联网上很少见，因为大家更偏爱成功故事——「上线即爆火」「一个人三个月 ARR 十万美元」。但真正做过东西的人都知道，现实里大部分项目不会成功。很多产品上线后没用户、没增长、没转化，开发者默默停掉服务器，项目就结束了。而这些失败经验，反而比成功学更有价值。
三、Builder 的日常，远没有想象中光鲜
互联网很容易把「独立开发」「AI 创业」包装得浪漫：一个人坐在咖啡馆里用 MacBook 敲代码，白天旅居，晚上收美元，产品自动增长，自由、松弛、充满未来感。
但真实世界里的 Builder，大部分时候没那么光鲜。更多时候是白天改需求，晚上修 bug；上线后发现支付流程坏了；landing page 改了五版，转化率还是很低；广告投出去，一个注册都没有；半夜两点还在查接口为什么突然报错；好不容易来了几个用户，一半还是朋友支持。
很多做过产品的人应该都经历过一个经典瞬间：熬夜两个星期终于上线，满脑子想着「会不会突然爆掉」，打开后台发现第一天总共十几个访问，大部分还是自己测试的。
那一瞬间挺打击人的。因为你第一次真正意识到，互联网不会因为你「很努力」就自动给你用户。
但也是从这个阶段开始，一个人才真正进入「做事情」的世界。你会慢慢明白，真正难的不是「想到一个点子」，而是后面那些没人愿意讲的东西：怎么持续迭代、怎么理解用户、怎么面对长期没有反馈、怎么在没人鼓掌的时候继续做下去。
如果长期只看网红，你很容易以为成功靠的是风口、流量和一次爆点。但如果你长期关注真正做事的人，你会发现真实世界非常朴素：有人做了二十个小产品，第二十一个才开始赚钱；有人持续发了半年内容，才接到第一个客户；有人把 onboarding 流程改了八次，留存率才终于提升。这些故事不刺激，也不容易传播，但它们会让你开始接受「慢慢来」这件事。
四、别只围观，开始动手
现在有一种很普遍的现象：很多人以为自己在「进入 AI 行业」，其实只是在围观。他们每天看最新模型、最新趋势，能聊很多概念，但真正需要动手时，始终停留在「等自己准备好」。
可问题是，很多能力本来就是做出来的。你不上线一个产品，就不会理解什么叫用户反馈；不真正服务客户，就不知道什么需求有人付费；不真正踩坑，就不知道什么问题最麻烦。
Builder 最大的不同在于，他们会先开始做。哪怕产品很小，哪怕做得粗糙，哪怕没人关注，哪怕最后失败。因为他们知道，真实反馈永远比空谈趋势更重要。
我不是说网红没价值——好的表达者依然重要，他们能帮更多人打开视野。但如果你真的想在 AI 时代做一点自己的事情，别只看别人讲世界，也多看看那些正在亲手做世界的人。
如果你不知道从哪里开始找到这些人，可以去 X 上搜 #buildinpublic 标签，去 Product Hunt 看每天有什么新产品上线，去 Indie Hackers 读创始人的真实故事，去即刻关注「独立开发者」话题。这些地方聚集着大量正在一边做、一边分享的人。
更重要的是，最好你自己也慢慢变成这种人。哪怕只是做一个很小的工具，自动化一个重复流程，接到第一个客户，赚到第一笔几十美元的收入，记录一次失败，认真写一次复盘。
这些事情，可能都比继续收藏十篇「AI 趋势分析」更有价值。
因为 AI 时代真正拉开人与人差距的，可能已经不是谁最懂趋势，而是谁开始真正动手了。

现在有一种很普遍的现象：很多人以为自己在「进入 AI 行业」，其实只是在围观。他们每天看最新模型、最新趋势，能聊很多概念，但真正需要动手时，始终停留在「等自己准备好」。
可问题是，很多能力本来就是做出来的。你不上线一个产品，就不会理解什么叫用户反馈；不真正服务客户，就不知道什么需求有人付费；不真正踩坑，就不知道什么问题最麻烦。
Builder 最大的不同在于，他们会先开始做。哪怕产品很小，哪怕做得粗糙，哪怕没人关注，哪怕最后失败。因为他们知道，真实反馈永远比空谈趋势更重要。
我不是说网红没价值——好的表达者依然重要，他们能帮更多人打开视野。但如果你真的想在 AI 时代做一点自己的事情，别只看别人讲世界，也多看看那些正在亲手做世界的人。
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIdt7rhX0AAKCzA?format=jpg&name=small)](https://x.com/i/article/2055613452798902272/Xudong07452910/article/2055904097358794948/media/2055732626980327424)
如果你不知道从哪里开始找到这些人，可以去 X 上搜
[#buildinpublic](https://x.com/search?q=%23buildinpublic&src=hashtag%5Fclick)
标签，去 Product Hunt 看每天有什么新产品上线，去 Indie Hacker

> 选择关注谁，决定你会成为什么。
最近这一年，我越来越明显地感觉到一件事：很多人每天都在高强度「关注 AI」，但真正开始动手做东西的人，其实并不多。
每天打开 X、小红书、YouTube，你都会看到大量关于 AI 的内容。有人分析行业趋势，有人预测未来职业，有人讨论 Agent 会如何改变世界，也有人不断强调「普通人最后的机会来了」。
这些内容本身并没有问题。很多人讲得确实好，逻辑清晰，表达有感染力，也帮助了不少人第一次接触 AI。
但看久了之后，你会慢慢产生一种奇怪的感觉：你好像知道了很多东西，却又什么都没有真正开始。
你收藏了几十篇「AI 创业指南」，关注了一堆「未来趋势」博主，也记住了大量热门词汇——MCP、Agent、Workflow、RAG、Multi-Agent。可回头看时会发现，自己真正做过的事情其实很少。
这种状态我自己也经历过。有段时间，我每天刷大量 AI 内容，今天有人说「AI 将淘汰程序员」，明天有人说「一个人公司时代来了」，后天又有人说「未来属于超级个体」。每句话都让人产生「再不行动就晚了」的紧迫感，可真正让我开始改变的，并不是那些宏大的观点，而是后来我越来越多地开始关注一些真正下场做事的人。
##
一、网红讲趋势，Builder 讲怎么做
网红的价值一直存在。他们擅长总结趋势、提炼观点、放大情绪，能让更多人第一次理解 AI 到底意味着什么。
但大部分趋势内容有一个共同特点：它们更像一种「认知消费品」。你看的时候很兴奋，觉得自己已经理解了这个时代，但这种理解往往停留在观点层面，不会真正转化成行动。
比如有人会不断告诉你：「未来一定属于 Agent」「AI 会重构所有行业」「不会用 AI 的人会被淘汰」。这些话可能都没错，但对于真正想做事的人来说，他更关心的问题是：Agent 到底解决了什么真实需求？用户为什么愿意付费？什么场景是真的高频？一个普通人应该从哪里开始？
这些问题，往往只有真正做过产品的人才会聊。因为它们不是观点，而是经验。经验这种东西通常不够「性感」，甚至有点狼狈，但恰恰最接近真实世界。
##
二、Builder 的分享，会让你第一次认真想「怎么做」
我现在越来越喜欢看独立开发者的分享，原因很简单：他们讲的东西通常格外具体。
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIdtwJ_WUAAUnYJ?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2055613452798902272/Xudong07452910/article/2055904097358794948/media/2055732429000691712)
前段时间我看到一个开发者分享，说他最开始做 AI 产品时，一直以为用户最需要「AI 帮忙生成内容」，于是花了很多时间做 AI 写作、AI 总结之类的功能，技术做得不差，但用户始终不愿意付费。后来他偶然接触到一些跨境电商卖家，发现这些人每天都在重复做一件枯燥的事：整理 SKU、填写产品信息、同步平台数据。于是他花了一个周末，做了一个帮卖家自动整理商品表格的小工具。界面不漂亮，功能也不复杂，但上线后很快就有了付费用户。
这个例子让我印象极深。因为它说明真实市场和想象中的市场完全不一样——很多付费需求，不过是帮别人节省一点时间，减少一点重复劳动。
类似的还有一个人的经历：他最开始迷恋「做大产品」，想做平台、做生态、做所有人都会用的 AI 应用。折腾了大半年，功能越来越多，系统越来越复杂，但始终没人真正留下来。最后反而靠一个很小的功能活了下来：帮用户自动把会议录音整理成客户沟通纪要。这功能一点都不酷，也没有什么「AGI 感」，但因为它解决的是企业里每天都会出现的真实问题，用户愿意长期付费。
还有一种内容我现在尤其珍惜：那些坦率承认失败的分享。有人花了两个月做产品，发现根本没人用，决定关掉；有人认真复盘为什么广告投放毫无效果，为什么自以为很重要的功能用户根本不在意。
这种分享在互联网上很少见，因为大家更偏爱成功故事——「上线即爆火」「一个人三个月 ARR 十万美元」。但真正做过东西的人都知道，现实里大部分项目不会成功。很多产品上线后没用户、没增长、没转化，开发者默默停掉服务器，项目就结束了。而这些失败经验，反而比成功学更有价值。
##
三、Builder 的日常，远没有想象中光鲜
互联网很容易把「独立开发」「AI 创业」包装得浪漫：一个人坐在咖啡馆里用 MacBook 敲代码，白天旅居，晚上收美元，产品自动增长，自由、松弛、充满未来感。
但真实世界里的 Builder，大部分时候没那么光鲜。更多时候是白天改需求，晚上修 bug；上线后发现支付流程坏了；landing page 改了五版，转化率还是很低；广告投出去，一个注册都没有；半夜两点还在查接口为什么突然报错；好不容易来了几个用户，一半还是朋友支持。
很多做过产品的人应该都经历过一个经典瞬间：熬夜两个星期终于上线，满脑子想着「会不会突然爆掉」，打开后台发现第一天总共十几个访问，大部分还是自己测试的。
那一瞬间挺打击人的。因为你第一次真正意识到，互联网不会因为你「很努力」就自动给你用户。
但也是从这个阶段开始，一个人才真正进入「做事情」的世界。你会慢慢明白，真正难的不是「想到一个点子」，而是后面那些没人愿意讲的东西：怎么持续迭代、怎么理解用户、怎么面对长期没有反馈、怎么在没人鼓掌的时候继续做下去。
如果长期只看网红，你很容易以为成功靠的是风口、流量和一次爆点。但如果你长期关注真正做事的人，你会发现真实世界非常朴素：有人做了二十个小产品，第二十一个才开始赚钱；有人持续发了半年内容，才接到第一个客户；有人把 onboarding 流程改了八次，留存率才终于提升。这些故事不刺激，也不容易传播，但它们会让你开始接受「慢慢来」这件事。
##
四、别只围观，开始动手
现在有一种很普遍的现象：很多人以为自己在「进入 AI 行业」，其实只是在围观。他们每天看最新模型、最新趋势，能聊很多概念，但真正需要动手时，始终停留在「等自己准备好」。
可问题是，很多能力本来就是做出来的。你不上线一个产品，就不会理解什么叫用户反馈；不真正服务客户，就不知道什么需求有人付费；不真正踩坑，就不知道什么问题最麻烦。
Builder 最大的不同在于，他们会先开始做。哪怕产品很小，哪怕做得粗糙，哪怕没人关注，哪怕最后失败。因为他们知道，真实反馈永远比空谈趋势更重要。
我不是说网红没价值——好的表达者依然重要，他们能帮更多人打开视野。但如果你真的想在 AI 时代做一点自己的事情，别只看别人讲世界，也多看看那些正在亲手做世界的人。

item.content:encoded:
Vasilije (@tricalt)

http://x.com/i/article/2053986800050524160

📄 X Article: Memory isn't a plugin. Skills aren't a plugin. They're the same harness.

X Article full text (2,798 chars)
Memory APIs are not a viable product category, and skill systems are just markdown. We've been saying it for a while.
@sarahwooders and @hwchase17 made the case last month that memory isn't a plugin and that it is the harness instead.
I made the same argument earlier, from the other side. We argued in a post that got 1.7M views that skills aren't static files. Skills degrade silently in dynamic environments. They need a loop — Observe → Inspect → Amend → Evaluate.
Both arguments are in essence about the same harness. A world model.
Treat skills and memory as the same harness
A world model is whatever the agent is aware of and what it uses to predict the next action it should take. In an agent harness, it is a broad state of all things you touch: the codebase layout, the tool schemas, the file system, the last 20 turns of conversation and the user's preferences.
The world model is the entire aggregate of context that the harness loads to decide the next step.
You can look at memory as a broad harness and skill as a specific one.
Is skill a subset of memory?
Skills are the part that records what to do. A SKILL.md is a procedure-level claim: "to do task T, run steps X, Y, Z."
Skills extend memory with a practical ability to do N tasks. Skills are a compressed procedure. It says "the world has responded to X, Y, Z by producing T in the past, and probably will again."
Memory observes the world while skills codifies it into a rule.
We've extended cognee to store skills and memory in the same store. Self-improvement runtime and agentic retriever share the same graph nodes.
How Cognee handles it?
cognee.remember("skills/") now lets you ingest skills with one line.
Inside Cognee a SkillChangeEvent emits memory events when skill changes. The skill is a memory node that evolves, is traceable, and controllable.
Skills improve by reading their memory. Memory improves by amending the skills attached to it. There's no clean line between them because there should not be one.
We have recently organized a hackathon where users built 21 LLM Knowledge Wikis in 3 hours using Cognee and Redis as session store!
And they did so because it was quite easy to manage skills
Conclusion
Every world model outside board games is permanently misspecified. The harness's job isn't to fix the schema. It's to run a controller on top of one that's wrong by construction. Cognee is that controller, and skill self-improvement is the first step.
It doesn't matter if you use a memory api, skills, or an agent md file. Even compaction strategies are part of the same play.
It is the same world model.
The harness that wins treats memory and skills as one comprehensive world model from the start.
Imho, if your memory system can't route a skill, it's not memory, let alone a world model.

Memory APIs are not a viable product category, and skill systems are just markdown. We've been saying it for a while.
[@sarahwooders](https://x.com/@sarahwooders)
and
[@hwchase17](https://x.com/@hwchase17)
made the case last month that memory isn't a plugin and that it is the harness instead.
I made the same argument earlier, from the other side. We argued in a post that got 1.7M views that
[skills aren't static files](https://x.com/tricalt/status/2032179887277060476)
. Skills degrade silently in dynamic environments. They need a loop — Observe → Inspect → Amend → Evaluate.
Both arguments are in essence about the same harness. A world model.
##
Treat skills and memory as the same harness
A world model is whatever the agent is aware of and what it uses to predict the next action it should take. In an agent harness, it is a broad state of all things you touch: the codebase layout, the tool schemas, the file system, the last 20 turns of conversation and the user's preferences.
The world model is the entire aggregate of context that the harness loads to decide the next step.
You can look at memory as a broad harness and skill as a specific one.
##
Is skill a subset of memory?
Skills are the part that records what to do. A SKILL.md is a procedure-level claim: "to do task T, run steps X, Y, Z."
Skills extend memory with a practical ability to do N tasks. Skills are a compressed procedure. It says "the world has responded to X, Y, Z by producing T in the past, and probably will again."
Memory observes the world while skills codifies it into a rule.
We've extended cognee to store skills and memory in the same store. Self-improvement runtime and agentic retriever share the same graph nodes.
##
How Cognee handles it?
cognee.remember("skills/") now lets you ingest skills with one line.
Inside Cognee a SkillChangeEvent emits memory events when skill changes. The skill is a memory node that evolves, is traceable, and controllable.
Skills improve by reading their memory. Memory improves by amending the skills attached to it. There's no clean line between them because there should not be one.
We have recently organized a hackathon where users built 21 LLM Knowledge Wikis in 3 hours using Cognee and Redis as session store!
And they did so because improving skills and memory is trivial in our new API:
python
```python
proposal_result = await cognee.remember(
SkillRunEntry(
selected_skill_id=skill_to_improve,
task_text="Review the current skiill,
result_summary="Review missed boundary bug.",
success_score=score,
feedback=-1.0 if score < 0.7 else 1.0,
),
dataset_name=DATASET,
session_id=SESSION,
skill_improvement={
"skill_name": skill_to_improve,
"apply": False,
"score_threshold": 0.9,
},
)
```
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIfvVw4bkAAUfCy?format=jpg&name=small)](https://x.com/i/article/2053986800050524160/tricalt/article/2055876832797581406/media/2055874912095801344)

##
Is skill a subset of memory?
Skills are the part that records what to do. A SKILL.md is a procedure-level claim: "to do task T, run steps X, Y, Z."
Skills extend memory with a practical ability to do N tasks. Skills are a compressed procedure. It says "the world has responded to X, Y, Z by producing T in the past, and probably will again."
Memory observes the world while skills codifies it into a rule.
We've extended cognee to store skills and memory in the same store. Self-improvement runtime and agentic retriever share the same graph nodes.
##
How Cognee handles it?
cognee.remember("skills/") now lets you ingest skills with one line.
Inside Cognee a SkillChangeEvent emits memory events when skill changes. The skill is a memory node that evolves, is traceable, and controllable.
Skills improve by reading their memory. Memory improves by amending the skills attached to it. There's no clean line between them because there should not be one.
We have recently organized a hackathon where users built 21 LLM Knowledge Wikis in 3 hours using Cognee and Redis as session store!
And they did so because improving skills and memory is trivial in our new API:
python
```python
proposal_result = await cognee.remember(
SkillRunEntry(
selected_skill_id=skill_to_improve,
task_text="Review the current skiill,
result_summary="Review missed boundary bug.",
success_score=score,
feedback=-1.0 if score < 0.7 else 1.0,
),
dataset_name=DATASET,
session_id=SESSION,
skill_improvement={
"skill_name": skill_to_improve,
"apply": False,
"score_threshold": 0.9,
},
)
```

##
Conclusion

Lotte (@lotte_verheyden)

http://x.com/i/article/2054596954282496000

📄 X Article: Designing eval datasets for LLM applications

X Article full text (4,695 chars)
.This is one piece of a series we’re publishing as part of the Langfuse Academy, where we walk through the full AI engineering lifecycle. If you’re new to the series,The AI Engineering Loop is the best place to start
A short recap of the AI Engineering Loop
The AI Engineering Loop is how teams continuously improve AI systems. It connects what’s happening in production (tracing, monitoring) to structured iteration during development (datasets, experiments, evaluation). Each shipped improvement produces new data, and teams loop through this process continuously.
You can read more on this here.
How datasets fit into the loop
So far, we've covered the first two steps of the AI engineering loop: tracing your application and monitoring its behavior live. Those give you visibility into what your system is actually doing and give you inspiration for improvement.
Now the question becomes: when you spot something worth improving, how do you test a change before deploying it to production? The next three steps of the loop cover exactly this, and it starts with datasets.
A dataset is a collection of test cases that you run your application against each time you make a change ("an experiment"). Instead of deploying and hoping for the best, you get a repeatable, consistent check across a set of inputs that represent real-world usage.
The dataset item
A dataset is made up of items, each item represents one test case: a situation your application should be able to handle. Generally, an item has three fields:
Input (required)
Expected output (optional)
Metadata (optional)
The three fields of a dataset item
A good mental model:
Common expected output patterns
Whether you need an expected output, and what it looks like, depends on which type of evaluator you use.
Reference-based versus reference-free evaluators
Some evaluators check the output against a predefined expected output (reference-based). Others assess the output without needing a ground truth to compare against (reference-free).
Exact match
The expected output is the literal correct answer. For example:
A classification task where the correct label is "billing_inquiry"
An extraction task where the expected entities are ["Paris", "Thursday"]
Reference answer
The expected output is a gold-standard response that shows what a good output looks like. The evaluator can compare the test's output against this example, for instance by checking semantic similarity or whether the key points match.
Evaluation criteria
The expected output is a list of checks or requirements the output should satisfy. For example:
"must mention the refund policy"
"must include a link to the help center"
The evaluator checks whether the output meets these criteria.
Nothing
Sometimes no expected output is required at all. If you're just checking whether:
the tone is professional
the response is safe
the output follows a required format
Your dataset items don't need anything other than an input as you will use a reference-free evaluator.
Combination of the above
Because you can run a combination of different evaluators on a single dataset item, a dataset item's expected output field can also contain multiple types of reference data. The expected output is a JSON field, so you can store multiple types of reference data without a problem.
What makes a good dataset
A good dataset mirrors what your system will encounter in production. If passing the dataset gives you confidence before deploying, it's doing its job.
Clear in scope. Each dataset should have a well-defined scope. That can be end-to-end if you treat internal steps as implementation details, or it can target an individual step like retrieval or summarization if that's the part you're trying to improve. You'll likely end up with multiple datasets, each with a clear purpose.
The right size for the workflow. Some datasets are small and fast enough to run on every push as part of your CI/CD pipeline. Others are larger and more comprehensive, and are useful to run periodically but too slow for every minor change.
Where to start
Start with the most concrete examples you have, then expand coverage once you know what you are trying to test.
Pull examples from production traces that you spotted and would like to improve, either as-is or anonymized or transformed by AI.
Add hand-written cases based on predefined requirements, edge cases, or behaviors your agent must handle reliably.
Generate synthetic examples with AI once you know which dimensions you want to cover more broadly.
What comes next
Once you have a dataset, the next step is running your system against it to see how changes affect output quality. This is what experiments are for.

item.content:encoded:
Zayn Hao (@ZaynHao)

分享一下五年前写的一篇小短文，希望对使用 Web 技术来打造原生应用 UI 体验的朋友有所帮助，

其中有一些是围绕 使 PWA 应用更像 Native App 的场景。

1.为 PWA standalone 模式设置空标题。
2.使用 `display-mode` 来设置 PWA 专属样式。
3.设置取消滚动溢出，避免滚动到顶部时产生的间隙。
4.设置鼠标指针为默认 default，禁止用户选择。
5.为不同系统设置单独的应用图标。
6. 使用 `router.replace` 来处理路由导航。

https://fehey.com/5-pwa-tips

🔗 使 PWA 更像 Native App 的 6 个技巧 · 在杂草中

21 / 11 / 18 使 PWA 更像 Native App 的 6 个技巧 你在开发 PWA 吗？此篇介绍几个通过 JavaScript 和 CSS 就可以使你的 PWA 更接近 Native 应用的小技巧。 1. 为 PWA standalone 模式设置空标题 。 网页的 Title 在浏览器访问场景下有着重要的作用，尤其是当打开了多个标签页时，可以根据 Title 来快速区分不同的网页。另外一点，聪明的网页开发者经常在 Title 中设置适当的信息以利好 SEO。 而 PWA 以 standalone 模式使用时，由于其拥有自己独立的窗口、独立的启动器图标等，此时 Title 便可能不那么重要了。所以为了使其更干净，更接近 Native App，可以单独为此模式访问时设置简洁的标题，甚至不设置标题，减少页面文字元素干扰。 const mqStandAlone = '(display-mode: standalone)' // Check this page is running in pwa mode if (navigator.standalone || window.matchMedia(mqStandAlone)) { document.title = '' } navigator.standalone 是检测网页是否以独立模式运行，其仅在 iOS Safari 浏览器上收到支持。 详情见： navigator.standalone MDN 2. 使用 display-mode 来设置 PWA 专属样式 。 例如这样设置一个圆角，使浏览器 Title 区域和网页导航部分更加融为一体。而浏览器模式时，则不需要此圆角，以避免圆角与浏览器边缘相遇时的消失凹陷。 < meta name = " theme-color " content = " #f5f5f5 " /> < style > nav { background-color : #f5f5f5 ; } main { backgrround-color : #fff ; } @media all and ( display-mode : standalone ) { main { border-top-left-radius : 12 px ; } } </ style > < body > < nav > </ nav > < main > </ main > </ body > 另外注意，我们这里使用 theme-color 来设置浏览器状态栏的背景色。 3. 设置取消滚动溢出，避免滚动到顶部时产生的间隙 。 按技巧 2 设置了之后，我们发现当滚动到网页顶部或底部边界时，浏览器默认的滚动溢出行为，会使我们网页中出现一条缝隙。我们可以使用下面这个设置来避免这一表现。 body { overscroll-behavior-y : none ; } 4. 设置鼠标指针为默认 default，禁止用户选择 。 这一技巧，在页面充斥大量的菜单和按钮，而非跳转性链接时，尤为有效。同时避免鼠标指针频繁地在默认和 point 状态来回跳动。 * , a , button { cursor : default ; user-select : none ; } 有网友认为，此做法有些偏激，但只是使其更接近 Native 应用而已。现在网站越来越模糊了按钮和链接的界限。通常情况下，按钮会具有较强的 UI 特征标识，链接仅从静态视觉看上去相对按钮来说会偏弱。 所以我们进行这一设置之后，可以为需要跳转页面的链接，再单独设置 cursor: point 即可。 5. 为不同系统设置单独的应用图标 。 例如为 PWA 独立应用模式访问时，在 Mac 系统场景下，设置一个 BigSure 风格的图标，浏览器访问则使用通用风格图标。下面一段简单的介绍来实现这一点。 我们需要两个单独的 manifest.json 文件，一个是通用配置文件，另一个是专门用于 Mac 的文件。 首先，从 HTML 页面删除 manifest link 的 href 属性 < link rel = " manifest " id = " manifest " /> 然后，使用 JavaScript 来检查是否是 Mac，然后根据结果来设置 href。 const setManifest = ( ) => { const isMacOS = / Mac OS X / . test ( navigator . userAgent ) document . querySelector ( '#manifest' ) . setAttribute ( 'href' , isMacOS ? '/manifest-mac.json' : '/manifest.json' ) } 对应的文件： // manifest.json { "short_name" : "YourProductName" , "name" : "YourProductName" , "description" : "Your information" , "icons" : [ { "src" : "/icon/android-icon-192*192.png" , "sizes" : "192*192" , "type" : "image/png" } , { "src" : "/icon/android-icon-512*512.png" , "sizes" : "512*512" , "type" : "image/png" } ] } // manifest-mac.json { "short_name" : "YourProductName" , "name" : "YourProductName" , "description" : "Your information" , "icons" : [ { "src" : "/icon/mac-icon.png" , "sizes" : "192*192" , "type" : "image/png" } , ] } 使用 router.replace 来处理路由导航 。 避免在移动端左右边缘滑动时的页面跳转行为，只有当需要提供「返回」功能时，再显式设置。 好了，以上就是我本次要分享的全部内容了，希望可以帮助你在进行 PWA 开发时，更好的处理一些细节。 “ 如果你想有任何想法，欢迎在 X/Twitter 上联系我。 ” Zayn Hao Gridea & Minttr's Founder Powered by Gridea
